title: regexp match/split size the wchar-to-multibyte conversion buffer by the input's byte length, which is not an upper bound for invalidly encoded input
live_proof: upstream e91dcfccaa, "Fix potential buffer overrun in regexp match/split functions", which postdates the 17.5 pin. Five lines of src/backend/utils/adt/regexp.c establish it on the pin. :1444 -- pg_mb2wchar_with_len() converts the subject string and, as upstream states, silently accepts bytes that are invalid in the database encoding, turning each such byte into one pg_wchar. :1579 -- maxsiz = eml * (int64) maxlen is the honest worst case. :1592-1593 -- `if (maxsiz > orig_len) conv_bufsiz = orig_len + 1;` throws that worst case away and caps the buffer at the subject's own byte length, on the assumption that converting back cannot produce more bytes than came in. That assumption holds only for valid input: one invalid byte becomes one pg_wchar, and pg_wchar2mb_with_len can spend more than one byte re-encoding it. :1597 -- the undersized buffer is palloc'd. :1644-1648 and :1793-1815 -- the two write sites call pg_wchar2mb_with_len into that buffer and check the result only with `Assert(len < matchctx->conv_bufsiz)`, which a non-assert build compiles out. The overrun is up to the subject's own length.
fidelity: real server, core, real allocator; reached by a C caller rather than by SQL. A subject of 64 bytes of 0x80, each invalid as a UTF8 lead byte. pg_mb2wchar_with_len turns each into one pg_wchar and pg_wchar2mb_with_len spends two bytes putting it back, so 64 bytes in become 128 out against the conv_buf of orig_len + 1 = 65 that regexp.c:1592 settled on.

status: measured on all three arms 2026-10-06: spatial=silent, sublet=detected, cheribsd-revocation=silent
note: Reached by a C caller inside the backend, not by SQL. No SQL statement reaches this defect: it needs a multibyte database encoding and an invalid byte sequence stored at the same time, and those are mutually exclusive in PostgreSQL -- measured against a native 17.5 cluster on 2026-10-06, where a UTF8 database refused invalid bytes on every route, convert_from(bytea,'LATIN1') produced valid UTF-8, and a SQL_ASCII database had pg_encoding_max_length 1, which skips the branch. Upstream guards one of the two with Assert rather than a runtime check, which says the same thing. palloc does not validate, so the corpus module at ports/postgres/app/reach-module builds the datum and hands it to the defective code, which is how upstream's own note about already-corrupt on-disk data describes it being reached. What the arms then measure is the memory safety of the defective code once reached, not SQL-level exploitability. Reached and witnessed on the host cassert ASan build on 2026-10-06: TRAP: failed Assert("len < matchctx->conv_bufsiz"), src/backend/utils/adt/regexp.c:1648, with regexp_match+0x510 in the stack. That is one of the two write sites named in PROVENANCE.md, and the assertion is the only check a non-assert build compiles out.
nested_why: The object is a palloc chunk, which AllocSet carves out of a block it took from malloc, so the defect is nested by the allocator that served it.
